text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The Swedish state risks being taken before a European court over an incident in 1995 where two policemen allegedly beat a man, Osmo Vallo, to death.

- Over 400,000 shareholders of mortgage bank Stadshypotek are being forced to pay 125 crowns to the company in an annual charge even though it is likely to be taken over by Handelsbanken next month. The bank has not said a word about picking up the tab, which totals 50 million crowns.
- Property company Realia rose strongly on the Stockholm bourse on Thursday after buying 20 properties from Securum's company Kungsleden.

- The international commission of inquiry's report about the Baltic Sea ferry disaster, in which hundreds of people died when the ferry Estonia went under in the autumn of 1994, will be delayed further. After having been postponed several times, the report was supposed to be presented during the first quarter of 1997, but no one really believes that will be possible, according to the paper.

- Swedish automotive group AB Volvo's deliveries of heavy and mid-sized trucks fell by about 16 percent to about 64,000 vehicles during 1996. Almost all of the downturn was seen in North and South America, while Volvo's truck unit managed to keep its European sales volumes, according to the paper's estimates.

- Economically, 1997 will be tough for Sweden, according to a report by the Swedish industrial association, which will be released next week. Thereby the association again has the gloomiest outlook of Swedish forecasters.

- Unemployment in Sweden continues to looks bad with 600,000 people or 13.4 percent out of work. During the first two weeks of 1997, 2,746 Swedes nationwide were warned that they will lose their jobs which is about the same level as in January 1996. These include workers at Ericsson, Volvo and Orrefors Kosta Boda.

- The management of Stockholm based trading and industrial group Hexagon, which bought AKA Industriprodukter and Swepart last year, is keen to make new corporate acquisitions. Chairman Torbjorn Ek says he is encouraged to act now with inflation and interest rates low.

- Clothing retailer Hennes & Mauritz is to open five stores in Finland in the second half of 1997. President Stefan Persson said this company will also this year test a new clothing store concept on the Swedish market with a smaller number of produts and less floor space.
